topic: Thread Design: Ensuring Unjoinability on All Scope Exits
explanation: Because destroying a joinable thread terminates the program, the developer must ensure that every possible path out of the scope where a `std::thread` object is defined—including normal flow, `return`, `continue`, `break`, `goto`, and exceptions—results in the thread being made unjoinable (via `join()` or `detach`). This requirement puts a significant onus on the programmer and is best solved by utilizing the RAII idiom, typically through a custom thread guard class (or `std::jthread` in C++20) that automatically calls `join()` or `detach()` in its destructor.
practical_example: In a function with complex branching logic, a developer uses `std::thread` but only calls `join()` at the very end of the function body. If an early `return` or `goto` statement is introduced later during maintenance, the thread skips the join call, leading to termination when the thread object is destroyed.
chapter: Item 37: Remember to make std::threads unjoinable on all paths
book: Effective Modern C++ by Scott Meyers
